chapter.learnerQuestion: After rain or dew, what is happening inside the flower and sheltered canopy, how long does moisture persist, and is the observed pattern consistent with rising disease risk or another cause?

sourceContext.citation: Punja ZK, Ni L, Lung S, Buirs L. Total yeast and mold levels in high THC-containing cannabis (Cannabis sativa L.) inflorescences are influenced by genotype, environment, and pre-and post-harvest handling practices. Frontiers in Microbiology. 2023;14:1192035. doi:10.3389/fmicb.2023.1192035.
sourceContext.supports: Cannabis inflorescence temperature and relative humidity can exceed nearby ambient conditions; genotype, inflorescence structure, air circulation, temperature and humidity all affected microbial load in the reported work.

sourceContext.citation: Punja ZK. Emerging diseases of Cannabis sativa and sustainable management. Pest Management Science. 2021.
sourceContext.supports: Botrytis bud rot can be severe under cool, wet field weather. Disease management depends on reducing moisture deposition, favorable humidity and pathogen spread rather than relying on a single ambient reading.

sourceContext.citation: Punja ZK, Collyer D, Scott C, Lung S, Holmes J, Sutton D. Fungal and mycotoxin contaminants in cannabis and hemp flowers: implications for consumer health and directions for further research. Frontiers in Microbiology. 2023;14:1278189.
sourceContext.supports: Cannabis and hemp inflorescences provide humid ecological niches for fungi, damaged tissues can be colonized under favorable conditions, and reducing humidity and spore spread can reduce fungal development.

subtopics.lessonTitle: Measure the flower microclimate instead of assuming ambient RH describes it
subtopics.goal: Quantify temperature and humidity at representative inflorescences and compare those readings with nearby ambient conditions so hidden humid zones are visible.

measure.method: Using a compact calibrated temperature/RH probe appropriate for the space, measure inside a representative dense inflorescence without crushing tissue. Record insertion location and allow the sensor to stabilize according to its response time.
measure.frequency: At consistent morning, midday and evening checkpoints during representative dry and humid periods; repeat after rain or dew events.

measure.method: Measure adjacent to the same plant at comparable height but outside the flower boundary, using the same instrument when practical.
Record temperature from the same probe and location used for flower RH. Avoid treating a nearby weather-station temperature as flower temperature.
measure.frequency: Paired with every flower RH measurement.

measure.method: Measure adjacent air temperature at the same plant height and time as the flower reading.

record: sensor model / calibration status / stabilization method
recent rain, dew, irrigation or fog exposure
compare: inside-flower vs adjacent ambient readings from the same time
dense vs more open flowers on the same plant or cohort
morning vs afternoon vs evening measurements
pre-rain vs post-rain/dew vs recovered dry-period measurements
interpret: A lower ambient RH does not prove the flower interior is equally dry; sheltered tissues can retain a different microclimate.
Repeated positive flower-to-ambient RH differences identify zones that deserve closer wetness and disease inspection, but they do not diagnose disease by themselves.
Genotype and flower architecture can change internal microclimate, so comparisons should preserve plant identity and developmental stage.
subtopics.decisionRule: Escalate monitoring and drying-risk inspection when the same flowers repeatedly remain more humid or warmer than comparison flowers after wet events. Do not assign a universal RH cutoff as a stand-alone disease diagnosis.
subtopics.confidenceCheck: Probe placement, response time and disturbance can affect readings. High-confidence comparisons use the same calibrated instrument, repeated locations and paired ambient measurements.

subtopics.lessonTitle: Track how long flowers stay wet after rain and dew
subtopics.goal: Measure wetting start, wetness persistence and drying opportunity so two rain events with similar totals are not treated as equivalent when the post-event environment differs.

measure.method: Record when rain, heavy dew, fog or overhead wetting begins and ends. Use on-site observation or a nearby weather record and label off-site data clearly.
measure.frequency: Every material flower-wetting event during susceptible flowering.

measure.method: Select marked flower positions and record the time from wetting end until the outer surfaces reach a consistent defined visibly-dry condition.
measure.frequency: Across representative rain and dew events.

measure.unit: minutes or hours or sensor wetness units
measure.method: Inspect the same sheltered flower zones at defined intervals. If using a wetness sensor, record sensor type, location and scale instead of converting its output to unsupported tissue-water values.
measure.frequency: At fixed intervals after wetting until the defined dry state returns.

measure.unit: RH, temperature, wind speed/direction, solar exposure
measure.method: Record paired local weather during the drying period, preferably at canopy height or with clearly labeled weather-station data.
measure.frequency: At wetting end and during the drying interval.

record: wetting source: rain / dew / fog / overhead water
event start/end and rainfall depth when available
ambient/flower RH and temperature where available
wind and solar exposure during drying
compare: events with similar rainfall but different drying weather
drying intervals before and after spacing/support/architecture changes
interpret: Rainfall total alone does not describe disease-weather pressure; duration of wetness and the environment after the event can differ substantially.
A flower that appears dry externally may still have a more humid interior, so visible drying and flower-microclimate measurements answer different questions.
Repeated wet events with incomplete drying between them deserve more attention than one isolated event followed by rapid drying.
subtopics.decisionRule: Use wetting duration plus post-event drying observations to prioritize scouting. Increase inspection frequency when sheltered flower zones repeatedly dry later than comparison zones or wet events recur before recovery.
subtopics.confidenceCheck: Visible dryness is a field screening definition, not a laboratory moisture measurement. Keep the definition consistent across events so trends remain comparable.

subtopics.lessonTitle: Map suspect flower symptoms before naming the disease
subtopics.goal: Quantify how many sampled flowers are affected, how severe the symptoms are, where they occur, and whether they are progressing before attributing the pattern to Botrytis or another cause.

measure.method: Inspect a defined sample of flowers using the same sampling pattern each round and record affected count divided by inspected count.
measure.frequency: Routine scouting and after prolonged wet or humid periods.

measure.method: Use a defined visual scale: 0 = no suspect tissue; 1 = small localized discoloration; 2 = multiple or locally expanding suspect areas; 3 = substantial flower tissue collapse or rot; 4 = extensive destruction or obvious fungal growth. Keep photo references for each class.
measure.frequency: Every affected flower recorded during scouting.

measure.method: Map affected plants and flower positions: outer/interior, upper/lower, windward/leeward, sheltered/exposed. Record clustering rather than only totals.

measure.unit: change in incidence/severity per defined interval
measure.method: Recheck marked suspect flowers or comparable sampling zones after a fixed interval and calculate the change.
measure.frequency: Shorten the interval when active progression is suspected; otherwise use the normal scouting cadence.

record: presence/absence of visible mycelium, sporulation, soft collapse or internal browning
physical injury / insect feeding / senescence look-alikes
compare: symptom incidence across exposed vs sheltered zones
affected vs unaffected flowers with similar weather exposure
suspect rot pattern vs physical injury, insect feeding and normal senescence observations
interpret: Browning or collapse is not uniquely diagnostic of Botrytis; tissue injury, insects, senescence and other pathogens can create overlapping appearances.
A clustered pattern following persistently wet sheltered zones provides different evidence than random isolated damage.
Increasing incidence and severity over repeated observations strengthens evidence of an active biological process but still may require laboratory confirmation for species-level diagnosis.
subtopics.decisionRule: Treat a symptom map as evidence for triage, not proof of pathogen identity. Escalate suspect biological disease when symptoms progress, cluster in favorable microclimates, or show characteristic fungal signs; preserve uncertainty when those features are absent.
subtopics.confidenceCheck: Visual diagnosis cannot reliably identify every pathogen to species. Laboratory microscopy, culture or molecular testing may be required when exact identification changes the decision.

subtopics.lessonTitle: Triage suspect flowers without turning inspection into a spread event
subtopics.goal: Record how suspect tissue is handled, whether sanitation steps are followed, and whether disease incidence changes after the response.

measure.unit: count per scouting or response event
measure.method: Record how many flowers or plants were flagged, isolated, sampled or removed according to the site's legal and operational protocol.

Use a checklist for tool changes or cleaning, glove/contact changes, and movement order from healthier to suspect zones where applicable. Record the approved product or procedure by reference rather than improvising concentrations on the field sheet.

measure.unit: % affected in the same sampling frame
measure.method: Repeat the same incidence survey after a defined interval and compare with the pre-response baseline.
measure.frequency: At the next planned scouting interval and sooner if progression is rapid.

measure.method: Map whether new suspect flowers appear adjacent to prior clusters, in the same sheltered zones, or elsewhere.

record: order of movement through the crop
material containment/disposal route according to local/site rules
photos and any laboratory sample IDs
compare: incidence/severity before vs after the response
areas handled with complete sanitation records vs missed or unknown steps
new symptom clusters relative to prior suspect areas and prevailing microclimate
interpret: A sanitation record helps determine whether handling practices could have contributed to spread, but correlation does not prove transmission route.
A decline in incidence after a response can coincide with drier weather or crop development; outcome should be interpreted with environmental context.
Chemical or biological treatment decisions require product legality, label compliance, crop stage and local rules; this field layer does not substitute for an approved pesticide program.
subtopics.decisionRule: Keep suspect-tissue handling traceable and re-measure outcome. If incidence continues to rise or new clusters appear despite improved drying conditions and sanitation, escalate diagnosis and management rather than repeating an unverified intervention.
subtopics.confidenceCheck: Before/after field observations are observational evidence. Strong causal claims require controlled comparison or diagnostic testing.

fieldWorksheet.title: Section 5 rain, flower microclimate & disease-risk field record
fields: incidence sample size / affected count / percent
visible fungal signs vs look-alike observations
decision and evidence needed to change it
fieldWorksheet.outcome: The learner should finish with a time-linked record connecting wetting, flower microclimate, drying, symptom distribution and response outcome instead of labeling any wet or browned flower as bud rot from appearance alone.

calculationHelpers.name: Flower-to-ambient RH difference
calculationHelpers.use: Compare hidden flower humidity with the surrounding air at the same time.
calculationHelpers.boundary: This difference is not a universal disease threshold and depends on probe placement, genotype, structure and weather.

calculationHelpers.name: Flower-to-ambient temperature difference
calculationHelpers.use: Track whether representative flowers consistently maintain a different temperature microclimate.
calculationHelpers.boundary: Temperature difference alone does not diagnose disease or moisture status.

calculationHelpers.name: Drying interval
calculationHelpers.formula: defined dry time − wetting end time
calculationHelpers.use: Compare drying opportunity among flowers, canopy zones and weather events.
calculationHelpers.boundary: A visibly dry exterior does not prove the inflorescence interior has reached the same humidity.

calculationHelpers.name: Symptom incidence
calculationHelpers.use: Track how widespread the observed symptom is in a defined sampling frame.
calculationHelpers.boundary: Incidence measures frequency, not severity or pathogen identity.

calculationHelpers.name: Incidence change
calculationHelpers.use: Describe whether the sampled symptom frequency increased or decreased after time or an intervention.
calculationHelpers.boundary: Observed change is not proof that the intervention caused the result because weather, sampling and crop development may also change.
